Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 56, verse 41–47:

Allah's saying: ﴿And the companions of the left — what are the companions of the left? — Amid scorching wind⁠ and boiling water⁠ and a shade of black smoke﴾ — "scorching wind" means a hot wind; "boiling water" means hot water; "a shade of black smoke" means intensely black smoke. The Arabs say: "aswad yahmum" (intensely black, jet-black) when something is extremely black. Al-Dahhak said: "The Fire is black, its people are black, and everything in it is black." Ibn Kaysan said: "al-Yahmum" is one of the names of the Fire.

﴿Neither cool nor generous⁠﴾ — Qatadah said: "Neither cool in its abode, nor pleasant in its sight." Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: "Nor generous, nor fine, its counterpart being ﴿of every noble pair⁠﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 7]." Muqatil said: "Good."

﴿Indeed they had been before that⁠﴾ — meaning in the worldly life — ﴿affluent⁠﴾, pampered.

﴿And they used to persist⁠﴾ — remain steadfast — ﴿in the great violation⁠﴾ — the great sin, which is shirk (associating partners with Allah). Al-Sha'bi said: "al-hinth al-'azim" is the perjury of the oath taken to deceive (al-yamin al-ghamus). The meaning of this is that they used to swear that they would not be resurrected, and they lied in that.

﴿And they used to say: "When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?"⁠﴾ — Abu Ja'far, Nafi', al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read "a-idha" as an interrogative and "inna" without it; the others read both with the interrogative particle.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 56, verses 48–60:

﴿Or our forefathers of old?" Say: "Indeed, the former and the latter will surely be gathered together for the appointed time of a known day. Then indeed you, O you who go astray and deny, will surely eat from a tree of al-Zaqqum, and fill your bellies with it, and drink on top of it from boiling water, drinking like thirsty camels.﴾ The people of Medina, ʿĀṣim and Ḥamzah read "شُرْبَ" (shurba) with a ḍammah on the shīn. The rest read it with a fatḥah on the shīn. Both are two dialects. The fatḥah form is the maṣdar (verbal noun), and the ḍammah form is an ism (noun) functioning in the sense of the maṣdar, like "الضَّعْفِ" and "الضُّعْفِ" (al-ḍaʿf and al-ḍuʿf, weakness). "الْهِيمُ" (al-Hīm) means thirsty camels. ʿIkrimah and Qatādah said: al-Hīmān is a disease that afflicts camels, in which they are never satisfied, and they keep drinking until they perish. It is said: a camel is "أَهْيَمُ" (ahyam), a she-camel is "هَيْمَاءُ" (haymāʾ), and the camels are "هِيمٌ" (hīm). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn ʿUyaynah said: "الْهِيمُ" (al-Hīm) means easy sandy land.

﴿This is their hospitality on the Day of Recompense.﴾ That is, what has been mentioned of al-Zaqqum and boiling water, meaning their provision, their food, and what has been prepared for them, ﴿on the Day of Recompense﴾, the day on which they will be repaid for their deeds. Then He argued against them concerning resurrection by His saying: ﴿We created you﴾. Muqātil said: We created you when you were nothing, and you know this. ﴿Why then do you not affirm?﴾ That is, why do you not believe in the resurrection?

﴿Have you considered what you emit?﴾ That is, what you pour into the wombs of the drops of semen.

﴿Is it you who create it?﴾ That is, is it you who create what you emit as a human being? ﴿Or are We the Creators? We have decreed﴾. Ibn Kathīr read "قَدَّرْنَا" (qaddarnā) with a light dāl, and the rest read it with a shadda on the dāl. Both are two dialects. ﴿death among you﴾. Muqātil said: Among you is one who reaches old age, and among you is one who dies as a child or as a young man. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: Its meaning is that He has made the people of the heavens and the people of the earth equal in it. According to this, the meaning of "قَدَّرْنَا" (qaddarnā) is qaḍaynā (We have decreed).

﴿And We are not to be outdone﴾ — that is, not overcome, not unable to destroy you and replace you with the likes of you. This is His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿on condition that We replace your likenesses﴾.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 56, verse 74–78:

﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty.﴾

His saying, may He be Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾. Most of the exegetes (mufassirun) said: its meaning is "I swear," and "la" is extra (silah). ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar used to recite it as fa-la-uqsimu with emphasis (al-tahqiq). It was also said: His saying "fa-la" is a refutation of what the disbelievers said about the Qur'an, that it is sorcery, poetry and soothsaying; its meaning is: the matter is not as they say. Then He began the oath, saying: ﴿I swear by the positions of the stars﴾. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "bi-mawqi‘" in the singular (al-tawhid). The others recited "bi-mawaqi‘" in the plural (al-jam‘). Ibn ʿAbbas said: He meant the stars of the Qur'an, for it was sent down upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ piece by piece, in scattered stars (nujum). A group of the exegetes said: He meant the setting places of the stars and their falling places. ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah said: He meant their stations (manazil). al-Hasan said: He meant their dispersal and scattering on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And indeed it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾, meaning this Book, and it is the object of the oath.

﴿Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an﴾, honored and esteemed because it is the speech of Allah. Some of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma‘ani) said: "Karim" refers to one whose nature is to give abundant good.

﴿In a Book well-guarded﴾, preserved with Allah in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), protected from the devils.

**Al-Baghawi's commentary (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on Surah 56, verses 83–89:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Why then﴾, meaning "why not" (فَهَلَّا), ﴿when it reaches the throat﴾, meaning when the soul reaches the throat at the time of death.

﴿And you, at that moment, are looking on﴾. He means: and you, O people of the dead man, are looking at him, waiting to see when his soul will depart. It was also said that the meaning of His saying "looking on" is: looking at My command and My authority. You cannot repel it, and you possess nothing.

﴿And We are nearer to him than you﴾, in knowledge, power and sight. It was also said: Our messengers who take his soul are nearer to him than you, ﴿but you do not see﴾ those who attend him.

﴿Why then﴾, meaning "why not" (فَهَلَّا), ﴿if you are not to be judged﴾, that is, not owned or subject to authority. Most of them said: not held accountable and not recompensed.

﴿Would you not bring it back, if you are truthful?﴾ That is, would you not return the soul of this dead man to his body after it has reached the throat? He answered his saying "Why then, when it reaches the throat" and his saying "Why then, if you are not to be judged" with one answer. Similar to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then whenever guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38]. Both were answered with one answer. Its meaning: if the matter is as you say, that there is no resurrection, no reckoning and no God who recompenses, then why do you not return the soul of the one dear to you when it reaches the throat? If you cannot do that, then know that the matter belongs to other than you, namely God, may He be exalted and glorified, so believe in Him. Then He mentioned the categories of creatures at death and explained their ranks, saying:

﴿But if he is one of those brought near﴾, ﴿But if he is one of those brought near﴾, and they are the foremost (al-sabiqun).

﴿Then rest﴾ (فَرَوْحٌ). Ya'qub read "fa-rūḥ" with a ḍammah on the rā', while the rest read it with a fatḥah. As for the one who read it with a ḍammah, al-Hasan said its meaning is: his soul departs in fragrant basil (al-rayḥān). Qatadah said: al-rūḥ means mercy, that is, for him there is mercy. It was also said: its meaning is "then life and endurance for them."

As for the one who read it with a fatḥah, its meaning is: then for him there is rawḥ, which is ease (al-rāḥah). This is the saying of Mujahid. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: it means joy (faraḥ). al-Dahhak said: forgiveness and mercy.

﴿And fragrance﴾ (رَيْحَانٌ), meaning rest (istirāḥah). Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: provision (rizq). Muqatil said: it is provision in the language of Himyar; it is said: "I went out seeking rayḥān Allah," meaning the provision of God.

Others said: it is the sweet herb that is smelled. Abu al-Aliyah said: none of those brought near departs this world until a branch of the fragrant herb of Paradise is brought to him, and he smells it, and then his soul is taken.

[[Al-Tabari reported these sayings (27/211–212), then said, giving preference: "The most correct of these sayings in my view is the saying of the one who said that by rawḥ is meant joy, mercy and forgiveness, and its origin is from their saying: 'I found rawḥ,' when he finds a breeze to rest in from the distress of heat. As for al-rayḥān, in my view it is the herb with which one is greeted at death, as Abu al-Aliyah and al-Hasan said. Whoever said something like what they said is right, because that is the most prevalent and most apparent of its meanings."]]

﴿And a Garden of delight﴾. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: "rawḥ" is deliverance from the Fire, and "rayḥān" is entry into the abode of permanence.

Ibn Hibban authenticated it in *Mawarid al-Zam'an*, no. (2335), p. 580; al-Hakim: 1/501–502, and al-Dhahabi agreed with him. al-Bazzar narrated it from Abdullah ibn Amr with a good chain. See: *Majma' al-Zawa'id*: 1/94.]]

Abd al-Wahid al-Malihi informed us, saying: Abu Mansur Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Sam'an informed us: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Abd al-Jabbar al-Rayyani informed us: Humayd ibn Zanjawayh informed us: Yunus ibn Abd al-A'la informed us: Ibn Wahb informed us: al-Sarri ibn Yahya informed me that Shuja' narrated to him from Abu Tibah, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever recites Surat al-Waqi'ah every night will never be afflicted with poverty."

[[Narrated by al-Harith ibn Abi Usamah, and al-Busiri said: "al-Harith narrated it from al-Abbas ibn al-Fadl, and he is weak. Abu Ya'la narrated it with a chain whose narrators are trustworthy." See: *al-Matalib al-Aliyah*: 3/383 with the editor's note. In *al-Kafi al-Shaf*, p. 163, he said: "Then they differed about the vocalization of Abu Zabyah: according to al-Daraqutni, it is with an unpointed ta' followed by a ya' and then a ba', and that he is Isa ibn Sulayman al-Jurjani, and that his narration from Ibn Mas'ud is disconnected (munqati'). This is supported by the fact that al-Tha'labi narrated it through Abu Bakr al-Ataridi from al-Sarri from Shuja' from Abu Tibah al-Jurjani. According to al-Bayhaqi, it is with a pointed (mu'jamah) letter followed by a ba', then a ya', and he is unknown. Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: This is a munkar hadith, and I do not know Shuja'."]]

And Abu Tibah never abandoned it.
